passages.text: Autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations in LCP1 cause a syndromic neutropenia and immunodeficiency

Actin cytoskeleton defects underlie immuno-actinopathies. <sentence_start/>We identified three patients with heterozygous LCP1 gain-of-function mutations (L362F, A365D) causing activated LCP1-associated immunodeficiency syndrome, characterized by congenital neutropenia, variable combined immunodeficiency, and allergy. <sentence_start/>Patients' neutrophils show maturation arrest and excessive apoptosis, while T/B cells are reduced and functionally impaired. <sentence_start/>Patient-derived iPSCs, CRISPR-edited cells, and LCP1<sup>+/L362F</sup> mice replicate these defects. <sentence_start/>Mechanistically, mutant LCP1 hyper-bundles F-actin, inducing VDAC1 oligomerization and mitochondrial apoptosis. <sentence_start/>This study further establishes LCP1 as a regulator of immune cell fate and suggests targeting actin dynamics as therapy.
Introduction

The actin cytoskeleton plays a pivotal role in immune regulation by mediating cell migration, intercellular communication via surface receptors and soluble mediators, antigen processing, and nuclear functions.<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9438836" doi="10.1126/science.279.5350.509" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19965462" doi="10.1126/science.1175862" pmcid="PMC3677050" count="1">2</citation>, <citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26292640" doi="10.1038/nri3877" pmcid="PMC4869833" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18304005" doi="10.1146/annurev.immunol.26.021607.090347" count="1">4</citation> Genetic mutations affecting actin cytoskeleton components lead to inborn errors of immunity. <sentence_start/>Actin-related inborn errors of immunity are collectively termed immuno-actinopathies.<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24117828" doi="10.1111/imr.12114" pmcid="PMC3884764" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2021.750537" pmcid="PMC8634686" pmid="34867982" count="1"><sup>6</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Currently, over twenty distinct immuno-actinopathy variants have been identified.<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32846417" doi="10.1159/000509717" pmcid="PMC7879252" count="1">7</citation>, <citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36952639" doi="10.1182/blood.2022018486" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30565251" doi="10.1111/imr.12716" count="1">9</citation>

Actin filaments (filamentous actin/F-actin) polymerize from globular actin monomers (globular actin/G-actin) in a polarized manner.<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12600310" doi="10.1016/s0092-8674(03)00120-x" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Their remodeling is regulated by tissue-specific actin-binding proteins that mediate cellular functions.<citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27528696" doi="10.1091/mbc.E15-10-0728" pmcid="PMC4985253" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Lymphocyte cytosolic protein 1 (LCP1, also termed LPL, L-plastin, or plastin-2) mediates F-actin bundling.<citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24117812" doi="10.1111/imr.12102" pmcid="PMC3801223" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>As a member of the plastin family, LCP1 exists alongside T-plastin and I-plastin isoforms, each demonstrating distinct tissue distribution.<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/935173" pmcid="PMC3238366" pmid="22194750" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Notably, LCP1 is exclusively expressed in immune cells.<citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2012/935173" pmcid="PMC3238366" pmid="22194750" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Phosphorylation of LCP1 at Ser 5 promotes immune synapse formation during T lymphocyte activation.<citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2022.916137" pmcid="PMC9277003" pmid="35844504" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1491005" doi="10.1093/oxfordjournals.jbchem.a123929" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>While LCP1 deficiency in mice preserves neutrophil development and migration, it impairs bacterial killing and integrin-mediated respiratory bursts.<citation rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12871642" doi="10.1016/s1074-7613(03)00172-9" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The clinical significance of LCP1 mutations remains under investigation. <sentence_start/>Mahat et al reported a heterozygous LCP1 mutation (c.694 A>T, p.I232F) associated with severe congenital neutropenia.<citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34991157" doi="10.1182/bloodadvances.2021006398" pmcid="PMC9043934" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Although <italic>in vitro</italic> studies characterized this mutation, the functional consequences of LCP1-mediated F-actin dysregulation on human neutrophil and lymphocyte development require further elucidation.

We report three patients from two unrelated families with heterozygous LCP1 missense mutations presenting with congenital neutropenia, combined immunodeficiency, and allergic manifestations. <sentence_start/>Laboratory analysis revealed increased apoptosis, cell cycle abnormalities, impaired migration, and defective differentiation/maturation in neutrophils and lymphocytes, while lymphocyte proliferation remained intact. <sentence_start/>Elevated cellular F-actin levels suggest that these LCP1 mutations represent gain-of-function variants. <sentence_start/>Thus, LCP1 mutations should be considered in congenital neutropenia and combined immunodeficiency cases.
Materials and methods
Study patients

All participants or their parents in this study provided written informed consent to participate in a protocol approved by the Ethical Review Board of the Children's Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, and all sample collection was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Whole-exome sequencing

For whole-exome sequencing, the TrueSeq Rapid exome kit and the Illumina HiSeq 3000 system were employed for analysis, as previously outlined.<citation rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35997928" doi="10.1007/s10875-022-01347-w" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The data was sent to the Beijing MyGenostics Sequencing Company for analysis, using H19 as the reference genome.
Sanger sequencing

Genomic DNA from the patients, parents, and siblings was used to validate and segregate the variants by Sanger sequencing. <sentence_start/>The following primers were designed for LCP1 amplification and sequencing: Forward: 5′-GACTTTCTGATTTTGGTGCAGGT-3'; Reverse: 5′-ATGAACGCTTTGTTAATGGACG-3'. <sentence_start/>The following primers were used for LCP1<sup>+/L362F</sup> mouse sequencing identification: Forward: 5′-TTTCTCATGTTATGCCTGCTCACTC-3'; Reverse: 5′-CTTCGGGCCTGATTTTGGAATTG-3'. <sentence_start/>PCR products were sequenced by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China).
Lymphocyte proliferation

A total of 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were labeled with carboxyfluorescein diacetate succinimidyl ester (CFSE) for cell dye and cell proliferation assessment.<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2025.1653662" pmcid="PMC12463974" pmid="41019080" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Phytohemagglutinin (PHA) or CD3/28 was employed to stimulate T lymphocytes, while F(ab)2′ IgM with CpG was used to stimulate B lymphocytes. <sentence_start/>The cells were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO<sub>2</sub>, and 95% humidity for 72 h. <sentence_start/>The proliferation of T and B lymphocytes was evaluated using flow cytometry.
Cell cycle detection

The cell cycle detection kit (Beyotime, C1052) was used for cell cycle detection. <sentence_start/>In brief, 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> neutrophils or 2 × 10<sup>5</sup> B cells were initially pre-cooled with 1 mL of ice bath and subsequently fixed with 70% ethanol at 4 °C for 2 h. <sentence_start/>Following fixation, cells were stained with propidium iodide in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min and treated with RNase A. <sentence_start/>Data acquisition was carried out using the Celesta instrument (BD Biosciences), and subsequent analysis was performed using FlowJo version 10.3.
Apoptosis detection

To ascertain neutrophil apoptosis, 2 × 10<sup>5</sup> cells were stimulated for 16 h at 37 °C in a 5% CO<sub>2</sub> incubator in the presence or absence of 10 μg/mL of Fas-associated death domain (FAS). <sentence_start/>Apoptosis was detected using 7-AAD and Annexin V-FITC, or activated Caspase-3-FITC. <sentence_start/>For lymphocyte apoptosis, 5 μg/mL of CD3 and CD28 were employed to stimulate T cells, while 10 μg/mL of IgM was used to stimulate B cells. <sentence_start/>Cells were stimulated at 37 °C for 72 h. <sentence_start/>Before apoptosis detection, cells were initially stained with CD4, CD8, and CD19 for gating purposes.
Migration assays

After HeLa cells had reached confluence in 6-well culture plates, uniform wound scratch lines were created within the designated locations using a pipette tip. <sentence_start/>Images of the scratches were captured at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h using an Upright fluorescence microscope (Nikon). <sentence_start/>The wound gaps were measured using ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health). <sentence_start/>For Transwell assays, 5 × 10<sup>5</sup> PBMCs were seeded onto a 5 μm Transwell chamber (Corning) in the presence of scalar dilutions of stromal cell-derived factor 1 alpha (SDF1-α, Peprotech), and migration capacity was assessed after 4-6 h.<citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30254128" doi="10.1182/blood-2018-07-863431" pmcid="PMC6265646" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>For mouse bone marrow neutrophils, 5 × 105 cells were seeded onto a 5 μm Transwell chamber in the presence of scalar dilutions of CXC motif chemokine ligand 1 (CXCL1, Peprotech) or N-formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine (fMLF, Sigma), and migration capacity was assessed after 4-6 h.
Western blotting experiment

The cycloheximide chase assay was adapted from a previous report. <sentence_start/>Briefly, HEK293T cells were plated and transfected with wild-type (WT), L362F, and A365D plasmids. <sentence_start/>Twenty-four hours later, cycloheximide was added (100 ng/mL), and cells were collected at different time points for Western blotting detection. <sentence_start/>For G-Actin/F-Actin <italic>in vivo</italic> assay, fractionation of F and G actin was performed following the manufacturer's protocols (BK037 Cytoskeleton). <sentence_start/>For the analysis of the T cell receptor (TCR) signaling pathway, 1 × 10<sup>6</sup> PBMCs were treated with or without 5 μg/mL CD3. <sentence_start/>PBMCs were lysed with protein splitting mixture, and then the supernatant was discarded by high-speed centrifugation to obtain protein. <sentence_start/>Proteins were separated by concentrated gel and separation gel, with LCP1 rabbit monoclonal antibody labeled, and an infrared imager was used for detection and analysis. <sentence_start/>Extracted cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline solution and immediately lysed for 30 min in RIPA buffer containing the protease inhibitor, phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF, Sigma-Aldrich). <sentence_start/>Supernatants were centrifuged at high speed into protein loading buffer and denatured at 95 °C. <sentence_start/>Protein lysates were subjected to SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore, Germany) for analysis. <sentence_start/>For the detection of voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1) oligomerization in mouse bone marrow neutrophils, Western blotting was performed using a primary antibody against VDAC1. <sentence_start/>In experiments involving inhibitors, they were administered 1 h (DIDS, Latrunculin B) and 12 h (Oroxylin A) before cell collection.
Confocal microscope

CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells were isolated from PBMCs using a separation kit (StemCell Technologies™) following standard protocols. <sentence_start/>The selected cells were suspended in a phosphate-buffered saline solution containing 2% fetal bovine serum and placed onto poly-<sc>l</sc>-lysine-coated slides for 45 min. <sentence_start/>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells were stimulated with mouse anti-human CD3 (Biolegend) and mouse anti-human CD28 (Biolegend) at 37 °C. <sentence_start/>The stimulation was halted at 0, 5, 10, and 20 min by adding 4% paraformaldehyde. <sentence_start/>Rabbit anti-human LCP1 primary antibodies were incubated overnight, F-actin was stained with Phalloidin-iFluor 488 (1:1000) (Abcam), and the cell nuclei were stained with DAPI (Beyotime). <sentence_start/>For neutrophils, cells were stimulated in the presence of 100 nM fMLF for 0, 1, 3, and 5 min. <sentence_start/>Analysis was carried out using a Nikon A1 confocal microscope. <sentence_start/>The average fluorescence intensity of each protein was measured using NIS-Elements AR 3.2 software. <sentence_start/>For immunofluorescence staining of mouse bone marrow neutrophils or induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neutrophils, cells were stained with primary antibodies against translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 (Tomm20) and VDAC1 for mitochondrial visualization and phalloidin for F-actin labeling; for inhibitor-treated groups, specific inhibitors were administered 1 h (DIDS, Latrunculin B) and 12 h (Oroxylin A) before cell collection, with all other analytical procedures performed as previously described.
iPSCs and neutrophil differentiation

PBMCs were cultivated in StemSpan™ SFEM II medium (STEMCELL Technologies) supplemented with several cytokines (stem cell factor, FLT-3, IL-3, and IL-6) for four days. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, the reprogramming procedure was executed using the CytoTune™-iPS 2.0 Sendai Reprogramming Kit (ThermoFisher Scientific).<citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.scr.2022.102822" pmid="35660815" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The transduced cells were subsequently transferred to plates coated with Matrigel (Corning Incorporated) and cultured in phosphoglucomutase 1 (PGM1) medium (Cellapy). <sentence_start/>After approximately 20 days, colonies resembling iPSCs were selected and expanded using PGM1 medium. <sentence_start/>For the differentiation of iPSCs into neutrophils, iPSCs were initially induced into CD34<sup>+</sup> hematopoietic progenitor cells using the STEMdiff Hematopoietic Kit (STEMCELL Technologies). <sentence_start/>Next, CD34<sup>+</sup> cells were resuspended in StemSpan SFEM II with 100 ng/mL of human stem cell factor, human thrombopoietin, and human Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3-ligand (PeproTech). <sentence_start/>Granulocytic differentiation was assessed by culturing cells in StemSpan SFEM II medium with 3 ng/mL granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF), 10 ng/mL of stem cell factor, and 10% fetal calf serum for 10-14 days.<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34115842" doi="10.1182/blood.2021010762" pmcid="PMC8814677" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23382209" doi="10.1073/pnas.1217039110" pmcid="PMC3581925" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> Granulocyte colony-forming unit assays were conducted using MethoCult H4230 (STEMCELL Technologies) supplemented with G-CSF and stem cell factor.<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15883170" doi="10.1084/jem.20041888" pmcid="PMC2212922" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation>
single-cell RNA-sequencing data analysis

Cryopreserved bone marrow mononuclear cells were isolated from patient 1 and two healthy controls (HCs) using Ficoll-Hypaque density gradient centrifugation. <sentence_start/>Single-cell RNA-sequencing libraries were prepared using 10 × Genomics Chromium Controller (v3 chemistry) following manufacturer protocols.

Raw sequencing data were processed with Cell Ranger (v6.1.2), with reads aligned to GRCh38 to generate feature-count matrices. <sentence_start/>Samples were merged initially to minimize batch effects. <sentence_start/>Cells containing ≥ 100 detected features were retained. <sentence_start/>Using Seurat (v4.3.0.1), we performed principal components analysis on the top 3000 variable features, followed by dimensional reduction and clustering (resolution = 2) using the top 30 principal components. <sentence_start/>After excluding clusters lacking cell-type-specific markers, 39,028 cells remained for analysis. <sentence_start/>Notably, HC2 was a 2.8-year-old male undergoing bone marrow collection during hospitalization for juvenile idiopathic arthritis, without evidence of immunodeficiency. <sentence_start/>Differential expression analysis employed Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests with Bonferroni correction. <sentence_start/>Significant genes underwent functional enrichment analysis via Metascape. <sentence_start/>Cell cycle phase assignment was based on module scores for S and G2M phase genes. <sentence_start/>G1 phase cells were identified from scatter plots of G2M versus S scores, with remaining cells classified as S or G2M phase based on established thresholds.
LCP1<sup>+/L362F</sup> mice

C57BL/6 <italic>LCP1</italic><sup>+/L362F</sup> knock-in mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome engineering by Cyagen Bioscience. <sentence_start/>In brief, the gRNA to the mouse Lcp1 gene, the donor vector containing "KI region-p.L362F(TTG to TTC)" cassette, and Cas9 mRNA were co-injected into fertilized mouse eggs to generate targeted knock-in offspring. <sentence_start/>F0 founder animals were identified by PCR followed by sequence analysis, which were bred to WT mice to test germline transmission and F1 animal generation.

gRNA target sequences were as follows: gRNA1 (matching forward strand of gene): GTTTACCACTGGCAGTATGGAGG; gRNA2 (matching reverse strand of gene): ATCAACCTCCATACTGCCAGTGG; gRNA3 (matching reverse strand of gene): GGGTGCATGCCGTGTGTGGCTGG; gRNA4 (matching reverse strand of gene): GACTGGGTGCATGCCGTGTGTGG.
All animal work was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Usage Committee of Children's Hospital of Chongqing Medical University.
Statistical analysis

Data analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 (GraphPad Software, USA), except for flow cytometry data, which were analyzed using FlowJo 10.3 (TreeStar Inc, USA). <sentence_start/>Statistical tests used were described in the figure legends. <sentence_start/>Statistical significance was defined as <italic>P</italic> < 0.05.
Results
Clinical manifestation
<italic>Family A</italic>

The index case (P1) is a 4-year-old male born to non-consanguineous parents. <sentence_start/>Samples were collected at age 2 years (born in June 2021). <sentence_start/>Growth and development were normal. <sentence_start/>Medical history included severe methicillin-resistant <italic>Staphylococcus aureus</italic> pneumonia requiring neonatal intensive care unit admission during the neonatal period, and hospitalization for rotavirus enteritis at 8 months. <sentence_start/>Five pneumonia episodes (respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, influenza virus, <italic>Streptococcus pneumoniae</italic>, and methicillin-resistant <italic>Staphylococcus aureus</italic>) required hospitalization but not intensive care (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers were noted. <sentence_start/>Hematologic evaluation revealed leukocytopenia, neutropenia, and lymphocytopenia, without anemia or thrombocytopenia. <sentence_start/>Absolute neutrophil count remained persistently below 0.5 × 10<sup>3</sup>/uL despite lymphocyte count fluctuations (Table S1). <sentence_start/>Serum IgA and IgM levels were decreased (Table 2). <sentence_start/>Initial evaluation for suspected severe congenital neutropenia showed no evidence of cyclicity on twice-weekly complete blood counts. <sentence_start/>Anti-neutrophil antibody testing was negative. <sentence_start/>Bone marrow examination at 3 months demonstrated hypocellularity with dysgranulopoiesis (myeloid-to-erythroid ratio: 1.3:1), showing granulocytic maturation arrest at promyelocyte and myelocyte stages (Fig. S1A; Table 1). <sentence_start/>G-CSF therapy (5 μg/kg) increased neutrophil count above 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>/uL, indicating a favorable response to G-CSF. <sentence_start/>Combined G-CSF and regular intravenous immunoglobulin therapy reduced infection frequency and severity. <sentence_start/>Repeat bone marrow examination at age 2.5 years showed a normal myeloid/erythroid ratio with a left-shifted granulocytic series and maturation up to band and segmented neutrophils, indicating resolution of prior granulocytic hypoplasia. <sentence_start/>Additional findings included severe allergic urticaria requiring oral steroids (Fig. 1A), incomplete left testicular descent, and right hydrocele. <sentence_start/>Vaccinations (hepatitis B, DTP, poliomyelitis, influenza) were tolerated with occasional mild fever. <sentence_start/>No live vaccines were administered.
Figure 1

Identification of heterozygous pathogenic mutations in the LCP1 gene in three patients with neutropenia and lymphopenia. <sentence_start/><bold>(A)</bold> Systemic allergic urticaria in P1 at age 2. <bold>(B)</bold> Bone marrow aspirate smear of P3 demonstrating granulocytic maturation arrest at promyelocyte/myelocyte stages and giant tetraploid karyotype neutrophils (Wright's stain, × 1000). <sentence_start/><bold>(C)</bold> Pedigrees of families A and B: affected individuals are shown in black; mutation carriers with uncertain phenotypes are shown in grey with question marks. <sentence_start/><bold>(D)</bold> Sanger sequencing of LCP1 mutation sites in families A and B, with mutated bases indicated by red font or arrows. <sentence_start/>P1 and P2 carry LCP1 c.1086G>C mutations. <sentence_start/>P3 and her father carry LCP1 c.1094C>A mutations. <sentence_start/><bold>(E)</bold> Amino acid residues conservation analysis of LCP1 mutations: L362 (yellow) and A365 (green). <sentence_start/>These two amino acid sites are highly conserved across different species. <sentence_start/><bold>(F, G)</bold> AlphaFold2-predicted 3D structure of LCP1 showing L362F and A365D within the horseshoe structure without disrupting hydrogen bonds, but increasing structural stability with potential actin-binding effects. <sentence_start/><bold>(H)</bold> Schematic of LCP1 protein domains with patient variants (red underline, yellow font) and previously reported I232F (blue font).

P2 (father of P1) had <italic>Haemophilus influenzae</italic> pneumonia, otitis media, recurrent oral ulcers, gingivitis, delayed wound healing, and allergies. <sentence_start/>Pulmonary tuberculosis was diagnosed at age 23. <sentence_start/>Whole-exome sequencing revealed no pathogenic mutations in Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial diseases (MSMD)-associated genes. <sentence_start/>Leukocyte, lymphocyte, and neutrophil counts were decreased. <sentence_start/>No other hematological abnormalities were observed. <sentence_start/>Bone marrow aspiration at age 22 showed decreased segmented neutrophils with increased promyelocytes and myelocytes, suggesting impaired granulocytic maturation (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Serial neutrophil measurements excluded cyclic neutropenia, and anti-neutrophil antibody tests were negative. <sentence_start/>Persistent neutrophil counts fluctuate within 0.5-1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>/uL, indicating chronic moderate neutropenia (Table S1). <sentence_start/>Without regular G-CSF therapy, he developed mild bronchiectasis and recurrent oral ulcers.
<italic>Family B</italic>

P3, a 4-year-old female, is the first child of non-consanguineous parents with normal growth parameters. <sentence_start/>At 7 months, she developed severe <italic>Staphylococcus aureus</italic> pneumonia requiring one month of hospitalization for intravenous antibiotics. <sentence_start/>Laboratory tests showed iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 76 g/L), neutropenia, and lymphocytopenia, without thrombocytopenia (Table S1). <sentence_start/>Bone marrow cytology at 9 months revealed granulocytic maturation arrest at promyelocyte/myelocyte stages, with 12% multinucleated immature granulocytes (Fig. 1B; Table 1). <sentence_start/>Repeat bone marrow examination at age 4 during gluteal cellulitis demonstrated hypoplastic granulopoiesis (myeloid-to-erythroid ratio: 0.29:1) with dysplasia and maturation arrest (Fig. S1B). <sentence_start/>The patient developed recurrent oral ulcers without regular G-CSF therapy. <sentence_start/>Clinical courses included three severe pneumonias (<italic>Staphylococcus aureus</italic>, <italic>Streptococcus pneumoniae</italic>, influenza virus), otitis media, and frequent upper respiratory infections (> 5/year) requiring intravenous antibiotics.
Identification of pathogenic LCP1 mutations

Whole-exome sequencing of P1 and family members revealed no severe congenital neutropenia-associated mutations per the 2024 update of the phenotypic classification by the International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS) expert committee on inborn errors of immunity.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.70962/jhi.20250003" pmcid="PMC12829761" pmid="41608114" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>A novel heterozygous LCP1 c.1086G>C (p.L362F) mutation was identified in P1 and P2, co-segregating with the disease phenotype (Fig. 1C and D). <sentence_start/>P3 carried a distinct heterozygous LCP1 c.1094C>A (p.A365D) mutation. <sentence_start/>Both variants exhibited high CADD pathogenicity scores (25.6 and 32, respectively) and were extremely rare (allele frequency < 0.0001) in the 1000 Genomes Database. <sentence_start/>Multiple prediction tools, including AlphaMissense, classified these mutations as deleterious/pathogenic (Table S2).<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37733863" doi="10.1126/science.adg7492" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The affected residues were evolutionarily conserved (Fig. 1E). <sentence_start/>AlphaFold2 analysis indicated preserved hydrogen bonding without structural disruption (Fig. 1F and G). <sentence_start/>Both mutations localized to a horseshoe-shaped F-actin interaction domain, adjacent to the previously reported I232F mutation within LCP1's actin-binding domain 1 (ABD1), though in distinct CH domains (Fig. 1H).<citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34991157" doi="10.1182/bloodadvances.2021006398" pmcid="PMC9043934" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Collectively, these data provide strong evidence implicating these LCP1 mutations in disease pathogenesis.
Impaired neutrophil differentiation, increased apoptosis, and cell cycle arrest

Given that neutropenia was the predominant feature in all patients, we performed comprehensive neutrophil analyses. <sentence_start/>Peripheral blood smears from P1 and P2 revealed elevated immature band neutrophils, along with increased eosinophil proportions. <sentence_start/>Flow cytometry demonstrated reduced mature neutrophil (CD16b<sup>+</sup>CD49d<sup>-</sup>) percentages and decreased CD11b/CD16 surface expression compared with HCs (Fig. 2A and B), consistent with our previous observations in patients with severe congenital neutropenia 1.<citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31176364" doi="10.1186/s12887-019-1556-x" pmcid="PMC6555947" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Functional assessments showed significantly higher apoptosis rates in patient neutrophils following 16 h <italic>in vitro</italic> stimulation with/without FAS or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) versus HCs (Fig. 2C and D). <sentence_start/>While dihydrorhodamine (DHR) staining revealed comparable respiratory burst capacity (Fig. 2E and F), enzyme assays indicated altered reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism: diminished intracellular O<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> production but elevated extracellular O<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> generation, suggesting dual dysregulation of endogenous and exogenous ROS pathways (Fig. 2G and H).Figure 2

Regarding long-term follow-up and prognosis in our patient cohort: among the three cases, none required hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with P2 surviving to adulthood. <sentence_start/>Treatment protocols included supportive care, antibiotic prophylaxis, and G-CSF administration to maintain neutrophil counts during acute infections. <sentence_start/>Notably, no patients developed myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia during follow-up, though long-term G-CSF use warrants continued surveillance. <sentence_start/>Potential therapeutic candidates include LCP1-specific inhibitors or actin polymerization blockers. <sentence_start/><italic>In vitro</italic> studies demonstrated Oroxylin A's efficacy in suppressing LCP1 mutant-induced F-actin elevation, supporting its therapeutic potential. <sentence_start/>Further screening of LCP1-specific inhibitors is recommended. <sentence_start/>The efficacy of regular intravenous immunoglobulin and anti-allergy therapies requires further investigation.

This study identified LCP1 gain-of-function mutations causing a primary immunodeficiency disorder, characterized by congenital neutropenia and combined immunodeficiency. <sentence_start/>Using patient-derived cells, LCP1-mutant cell lines, iPSCs, and mouse models, we demonstrated actin dysregulation mechanisms, revealing LCP1-regulated F-actin polymerization abnormalities. <sentence_start/>These models enable molecular mechanism investigation and therapeutic target identification.
